reason: A DEFECT THERE. A retired couple both 70 with $40,000 of Social Security and no other income: Indiana exempts the benefit, so federal AGI is zero and the $5,000 of exemptions takes Indiana AGI to MINUS $5,000. The whole difference is Marion County's 2.02% applied to that negative figure: `in_county_tax` is `rate * in_agi` with no floor, so PolicyEngine has an Indiana county paying a retiree $101 a year. It floors the STATE tax at zero on the same figure, which is what makes this an oversight rather than a reading of the statute. The other half of this difference used to be the unified tax credit for the elderly, IC 6-3-3-9 - $140, refundable, and the whole of an Indiana return for a household living on Social Security. It is modelled here from v0.22.0 and the two engines now agree on it to the cent, which is why this entry's bound fell from $250 to $110.

HARNESS. PolicyEngine computes the household's state and local tax and itemises when that beats the standard deduction; the harness supplies no itemised deductions, so this package takes the standard one. Above about $300,000 in a high-tax state the two diverge by the SALT deduction. Feeding a state tax back into the federal return is circular and the harness refuses to guess at it.
HARNESS. Follows the taxable-income difference above.

NOT MODELLED HERE. Colorado's Social Security subtraction (C.R.S. § 39-22-104(4)(f)), its child tax credit and its family affordability tax credit. The credits are large and refundable at low incomes; the subtraction makes a Colorado retiree too high. Recorded in the state's notes and in test/social-security.test.js.
NOT MODELLED HERE. Idaho's grocery credit ($155 a head, $155 more at 65) and its child tax credit, both named in the state's notes.
NOT MODELLED HERE. Arizona's family income tax credit (A.R.S. § 43-1073), $25 a person to $100 a return, and its $100 dependent tax credit.
NOT MODELLED HERE. Kentucky's family size tax credit, which forgives the whole tax below the federal poverty guideline for the household's size and phases out over the next 33%.

NOT UPDATED THERE, and the direction has REVERSED. Michigan's personal exemption is indexed annually under MCL 206.30(2), and for 2026 it is $5,900 - published in the state's own 2026 income tax withholding guide (Form 446, Rev. 02-26). This package carried the $5,800 of 2025 forward and flagged it provisional until Day 28; it now carries the published figure, and PolicyEngine-US PROJECTS $5,950 by uprating. So this entry used to describe a gap this package owed and now describes one it does not: the gap is $50 of exemption, $2.13 per exemption at 4.25%, and the side holding the published number is this one. The count went UP by one when the figure was corrected, which is worth understanding rather than explaining away - at $5,800 one household happened to land on the same rounded dollar as PolicyEngine's $5,950 and at $5,900 it no longer does. AGREEING WITH A PROJECTION IS NOT EVIDENCE, and a differential count that falls is not by itself a sign of being more right. Michigan's SPECIAL exemption for a blind or disabled filer is still carried forward at $3,400 and still flagged, because it appears on the MI-1040 and on no withholding document - see provisionalFigures on the state-year, which records that one figure rather than the whole year.

NOT MODELLED HERE. The Michigan home heating credit (MCL 206.527a), refundable and claimed on Form MI-1040CR-7, which pays a standard allowance by household size below an income ceiling and so reaches a low-income household with no heating bill on the return. PolicyEngine-US models it; this package does not. It appears only on the two lowest-income Michigan households in the grid.

A DERIVED RECAPTURE AGAINST A STORED ONE, and this entry used to say something false. It read 'NOT MODELLED THERE. The New York household credit ... PolicyEngine-US models neither the credit nor the offset' for as long as it has existed, and PolicyEngine-US models BOTH: ny_household_credit has been in its non-refundable credit list since 2007 and ny_eitc subtracts it under s 606(d)(1). Chasing that on Day 29 found TWO defects HERE, both now fixed, and closed every NY difference the entry was supposed to be about. (1) s 606(b) is measured on 'household gross income' -- the aggregate adjusted gross income of the household 'as reported for FEDERAL income tax purposes', which the IT-201 instructions make 'the amount from Form IT-201, line 19'. This package passed line 33, New York's own AGI, so every New York subtraction bought a credit whose ceiling is $32,000: a retired couple with $94,000 of federal AGI was given $75 of it. The locality engine had it right the whole time -- its parameter is named federalAgi, because the same instruction note covers the city tables. (2) IT-215 line 15 is 'the SMALLER of line 13 or line 14' -- Worksheet B line 5, or the household credit -- so the EIC is reduced only by the household credit the filer could USE. This package subtracted all of it, so a single parent of two at $12,000 lost $90 of a REFUNDABLE match to a NON-REFUNDABLE credit that could only ever have been worth $80. What is left under this entry is a different fact entirely, which is why the bound is now $2 rather than $80: this package DERIVES the s 601(d) supplemental tax from the rate schedule and PolicyEngine stores the published incremental-benefit table ($567 for a 2026 single filer). Inside the phase-in band the two differ by $1.06 at $150,000. WHICH IS RIGHT IS OPEN -- the table is written into the statute, so a derivation that disagrees with it by a dollar may be this package's defect rather than a rounding difference. It appears on no household with a household credit.

NOT MODELLED HERE. The North Carolina child deduction, up to $3,000 a child and phasing to zero as AGI rises (G.S. 105-153.5(a1)), named in the state's notes. The bound is $400 rather than $250 from Day 26, because the grid gained a household with THREE children and the deduction is per child: $9,000 at 3.99% is $359.10. North Carolina's retirement rules are now modelled: it taxes a pension in FULL and deducts military retired pay in full, which is why no retiree case is left here.

HARNESS. Massachusetts taxes its own gross income and the harness states it directly, so any difference is a difference about what belongs on Form 1 line 21 rather than about the tax. Massachusetts also has a No Tax Status and a Limited Income Credit that this package does not model.
HARNESS. Pennsylvania has no federal starting line, so the harness states the eight-class base itself.

PROVISIONAL FIGURES. Utah indexes the Taxpayer Tax Credit's phase-out threshold and its per-dependent exemption annually and had not published the 2026 amounts when this was written, so this package carries 2025's forward and says so. PolicyEngine has indexed values. The gap is 1.3 cents per dollar of threshold - $5.36 for a single filer, $10.73 joint - and will close when Utah publishes.

PROVISIONAL FIGURES. California's 2026 brackets, standard deduction and exemption credits are the 2025 published amounts carried forward; the FTB indexes them to the CCPI after this was written. PolicyEngine projects them.
NOT MODELLED HERE. Ohio's $20-per-exemption credit for a filer with Ohio AGI of $30,000 or less (R.C. 5747.022).

NOT UPDATED THERE, twice. Two facts, and between them they account for every Maryland difference in this grid to the cent - verified by running this package with both of PolicyEngine's figures, after which 22 of the 23 Maryland cases agreed exactly. (1) ALLEGANY COUNTY raised its rate from 3.03% to 3.20% for 2026. This package carries the new rate; PolicyEngine's county table cites the 2025 resident booklet and stops there, so it charges 2025's. That is 0.17 of a point of taxable income, which is why this entry is bounded by a SHARE OF INCOME rather than by a dollar figure: the same one fact is $43.76 on a $30,000 household and $678.70 on a $400,000 one. (2) The 2026 standard deduction, which until Day 28 was the other way round. HB 352 replaced the 15%-of-AGI formula with a flat $3,350/$6,700 indexed from 2026; this package carried the 2025 figure forward and flagged it provisional because secondary sources split between $3,350 and $3,400, and PolicyEngine uprates it to $3,400/$6,850. The Comptroller has settled it: the 2026 employer withholding guide and the 2026 Form MW507 both carry $3,350, and the fiscal note on HB 411 of 2026 - a bill to raise the deduction to $4,100, which died in committee - prices the rise against a current law of $3,350. So the figure never moved and PolicyEngine's is a projection of an increase that did not happen. At most $150 of deduction, about $6 of state and county tax at the top rate.

HARNESS, in the state. The same fact as the two federal entries above, one level down. At $400,000 PolicyEngine's household ITEMISES federally - its only itemised deduction being the state income tax it is in the middle of computing - and two states then follow that federal election, in both directions. VIRGINIA requires a federal itemiser to itemise on the state return (Va. Code § 58.1-322.03(1)) and subtracts state income tax from the itemised total, which in this harness leaves ZERO, so PolicyEngine gives the filer no deduction at all where this package gives the $8,750 standard one: $503.13 at 5.75%. GEORGIA does the same under § 48-7-27(a)(1), allowing $21,965 of itemised deductions against this package's $15,000 standard one, and then pays $300 a taxpayer for having itemised - the eligible itemizer credit of O.C.G.A. § 48-7-27.1, which IS modelled here from v0.22.0 and which test/georgia-itemizer-credit.test.js pins. It does not fire in this grid because the harness's own federal return takes the standard deduction, so `federal.deductionKind` is `standard` on every case in it. $347.55 of deduction plus $300 of credit is the $647.55. Neither difference can be closed from this harness, which supplies no itemised deductions on purpose: feeding a state tax back into the federal return is circular. NOTE the cite: this entry said § 48-7-29.23 until Day 26, copied from PolicyEngine-US's own variable file. No such section exists - their PARAMETER file has it right.

A DISAGREEMENT ABOUT AGE, and both models document their side. Mississippi exempts qualified retirement income under § 27-7-15(4)(k), and § 27-7-15(4)(l) leaves a PREMATURE distribution — one the federal § 72(t) penalty would reach — fully taxable. This package therefore requires 59 1/2; PolicyEngine-US models the exemption with no age test at all and says so in its own parameter file. The grid could not see the disagreement until Day 26, because every retiree in it was 67 or older. A 56-year-old drawing a $50,000 pension is charged $1,268 here and nothing there, and a couple of 57 and 55 with $70,000 is charged $1,736. This package's reading is in test/retirement-by-source.test.js and in the state's notes; it is the one place where being right costs the filer money, so it is worth restating that a distribution before 59 1/2 is what (l) is about.

§ 32(d), and a different reading of the ARPA amendment. A married filer who files separately gets no earned income credit under § 32(d)(1) unless § 32(d)(2) applies — which needs the filer to have lived with a qualifying child for more than half the year AND either to have had a different principal abode from the spouse for the last six months or to be legally separated and not a member of the same household. PolicyEngine-US turns a single parameter, `eligibility.separate_filer`, true from 2021 and allows the credit to EVERY separate filer. This package requires the facts: `separatedFromSpouse` plus a qualifying child, and the case grid supplies neither, so it computes zero. Neither model is reading the statute wrongly — one is assuming the exception applies and the other is assuming it does not, and nothing on a return either model was given says which. $1,053.62 for one child at $45,000 in 2026.

FOLLOWS THE § 32(d) DIFFERENCE ABOVE. Six states in this grid set their earned income credit as a flat percentage of the federal one, so a $1,053.62 disagreement about the federal credit reaches the state return multiplied by that state's match: New Jersey 40% ($421.45), New York 30% ($316.09), Illinois 20% plus its 40%-of-that child credit ($295.01 of it), Virginia 20% ($210.72), Indiana 10% ($105.36), and Maryland most of all, because Maryland matches at 50% AND every Maryland county runs its own earned income credit at ten times the county rate. The bound is $950 for that Maryland case. Not a state disagreement at all: fix the federal reading and all six move together.

GEORGIA HAS NO SURVIVING-SPOUSE AMOUNT -- the same reading as the $45,000 and the three high-income cases, and the case that shows the $748.50 those entries call a constant is not one. HB 1437 sets the standard deduction at one figure 'in the case of a married couple filing a joint return' and another 'in the case of any other taxpayer', so a surviving spouse takes the $15,000 and PolicyEngine-US gives the 2026 one the joint $30,000 while giving the 2025 one the single amount. Above $30,000 of income the whole $15,000 of difference is in use and the gap is $748.50 at every income. At $26,000 it is $299.40, because the widow has not got $30,000 of income for the larger deduction to come off: the difference is clipped by the income, not by the deduction. A DEDUCTION DISAGREEMENT IS A CONSTANT ONLY ABOVE THE DEDUCTION, which is exactly what a grid that only ever filed this status at $45,000 and up could not show. At $18,000 there is no difference at all -- both engines reach zero -- so the entry covers one case of the two.

GEORGIA HAS NO SURVIVING-SPOUSE AMOUNT, and this package follows the statute where PolicyEngine-US follows itself inconsistently. HB 1437 sets the standard deduction at one figure 'in the case of a married couple filing a joint return' and another 'in the case of any other taxpayer', so a surviving spouse takes the $15,000. PolicyEngine gives the 2026 surviving spouse the JOINT $30,000 while giving the 2025 one the SINGLE amount, which is what makes this a reading rather than a rate: $15,000 at 4.99% is $748.50. Recorded in Georgia's notes since v0.15.0.

A DEFECT THERE, and it was a defect HERE until Day 27. § 24(b)(2) sets the phase-out threshold at "$400,000 in the case of a joint return, and $200,000 in any other case". A QUALIFYING SURVIVING SPOUSE DOES NOT FILE A JOINT RETURN - § 2(a) hands them the joint RATE SCHEDULE under § 1(a) and says nothing about any threshold - so the figure is $200,000, and Schedule 8812 line 9 prints the same split in two lines: "Married filing jointly-$400,000" and "All other filing statuses-$200,000". PolicyEngine-US carries $400,000 for this status, so at $250,000 and $300,000 of wages it gives a widow with one child the full $2,200 and this package gives nothing. NOTE WHICH CASE IS MISSING FROM THIS LIST: at $450,000 the two engines AGREE at $0, because that income clears the joint threshold as well. That is the whole reason the $450,000 shape exists - without it, a report of two disagreeing incomes could not distinguish "this package now uses $200,000" from "this package lost the credit for some other reason". This package carried $400,000 too, with a comment calling the question UNRESOLVED on the grounds that irs.gov is blocked from the build sandbox and PolicyEngine agreed; the statutory sentence settles it unaided and was quoted in that comment. See packages/us-federal-tax/test/surviving-spouse.test.js, which walks the parameter tree and requires every status-keyed table in the package to declare its statutory grouping.

HARNESS. The same fact as the single-worker entry above, on the one surviving-spouse case rich enough to reach it: PolicyEngine computes the household's state and local tax and itemises when that beats the standard deduction, and the harness supplies no itemised deductions on purpose, so this package takes the standard one. It appears only in CALIFORNIA and MARYLAND, the two high-tax states in the grid where $450,000 of wages generates enough state and local tax to beat a $32,200 standard deduction. Feeding a state tax back into the federal return is circular and the harness refuses to guess at it.
HARNESS. Follows the taxable-income difference above.

GEORGIA HAS NO SURVIVING-SPOUSE AMOUNT - the same entry as the $45,000 surviving-spouse case, at three higher incomes. HB 1437 sets the standard deduction at one figure 'in the case of a married couple filing a joint return' and another 'in the case of any other taxpayer', so a surviving spouse takes the $15,000; PolicyEngine-US gives the 2026 surviving spouse the JOINT $30,000 while giving the 2025 one the SINGLE amount. It is $748.50 at EVERY income here - $15,000 of deduction at a flat 4.99% - which is what makes it a reading of the statute rather than a rate or a threshold, and is why one bound covers all three cases. A separate entry from the $45,000 one because `kind` matches exactly and the new shape is a new kind; that is a small cost of naming it `surviving-spouse-high` and it is worth paying, because a report that lumped the two together could not show that the $45,000 case and the $450,000 case differ by the same dollar.

CLOSED IN FOUR STATES AND STILL OPEN IN TWO, AND THE TWO THAT ARE LEFT ARE A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE ONE THIS ENTRY STARTED AS. Day 30 recorded six differences here as ONE open question: PolicyEngine-US counted the spouse in Virginia’s $930 personal exemption and $12,000 age deduction, Maryland’s $3,200 exemption and its $1,000 addition at 65, and Indiana’s $1,000 exemption and its $1,000 addition at 65, and this package counted nobody. Day 31 read the statutes and it was a defect HERE, as suspected - but the six differences were never one question. They were two, and only one of them is settled. THE EXEMPTION HALF IS CLOSED. IRC § 151(b) allows a separate filer an exemption for a spouse who has no gross income and is nobody else’s dependent, and four states in this package reach the same result by two different routes. Virginia (§ 58.1-322.03(1), "$930 for each personal exemption allowable to the taxpayer for FEDERAL income tax purposes") and Illinois (35 ILCS 5/204(b), the basic amount for each exemption allowable under § 151) point at the federal provision. Maryland (Tax-Gen. § 10-211) and Indiana (IC 6-3-1-3.5(a)) copy § 151(b)’s own sentence into their statutes. New Jersey expressly does NOT - N.J.S.A. 54A:3-1(b) conditions the spouse exemption on a joint return and attaches the "files no return" condition to a DOMESTIC PARTNER instead - so this is not a federal rule states inherit, and the answer is now declared per state with a per-state citation in ExemptionRule.separateReturnSpouse. The `separate-with-spouse-young` case had four differences at 61 and now has none, which is why that entry is gone. THE AGED HALF IS NOT SETTLED, AND IT IS NOT THE SAME CLAIM. A statute that made the spouse an exemption has not thereby made the spouse an AGED exemption - that inference is exactly the defect of 2026-09-24. Virginia settles it, and settles it by cross-reference: § 58.1-322.03(2)(b) gives the additional $800 to "each blind or aged taxpayer as defined under § 63(f)", and § 63(f)(1)(B) and (f)(2)(B) are the subparagraphs that reach this spouse through § 151(b). Maryland’s and Indiana’s $1,000 additions and Illinois’s are their own subdivisions written in their own words, nobody has read whose spouse they reach, the engine counts nobody there, and the result’s notes say so to any caller who supplied a spouseAge it then discarded. WHAT IS LEFT IS TWO DIFFERENCES. (1) INDIANA, $49.70 - the $1,000 age-65 addition for the spouse at the state rate plus an average county rate. That is the aged half above and it is one subdivision away from being read. (2) VIRGINIA, $690.01 - and this one was never the § 151(b) question at all. It is the $12,000 AGE DEDUCTION of § 58.1-322.03(5), which is not an exemption under § 151, is attached to a person’s own birth date rather than to an exemption count, and is withdrawn against a figure the Form 760 instructions compute from BOTH spouses on a separate return. $12,000 at Virginia’s 5.75% is $690.00. Deliberately not changed: PolicyEngine counts head and spouse for it with no filing-status test at all, and a deduction that is not an exemption cannot borrow the exemption’s citation. WHAT PolicyEngine’s SOURCE SAYS, which Day 30 could not check and Day 31 did. va_personal_exemption is `adds = ["va_personal_exemption_person"]` over a flat per-person amount with no filing-status logic anywhere in it; md_total_personal_exemptions is md_personal_exemption * tax_unit_size; in_base_exemptions is tax_unit_size * p.base.amount. All three are MEMBER COUNTS rather than readings of a form, and Virginia’s parameter file says so in words - "an income tax exemption of this value for each person in the filing unit". So PolicyEngine agreeing with the corrected answer here corroborates the arithmetic and is NOT evidence about the statute, and the four statutes were read independently of it. THAT DISTINCTION IS WHY THIS TOOK TWO DAYS RATHER THAN ONE, and it is the answer to Day 30’s "this harness cannot tell those apart": the harness cannot, but their source can, and it is a git clone away.
